newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ business weeklies - Jan 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ business weeklies - Jan 31.

text.p: Telecom and its subsidiary Digital Video Productions have slapped an injunction on the IDG computer publication Computerworld after it published graphical makeups of Wilson & Horton's Internet site. IDG alledged the Telecom subsidiary had not installed enough security on the computer containing its work in progress for the site. Page 1.

Telecom is facing fresh legal action on two fronts. BellSouth has lodged Commerce Act proceedings with the High Court at Auckland, alleging anti-competitive discounting practices and misuse of confidential BellSouth consumer information. And Clear Communications has filed a statement of claim in the High Court at Auckland alleging breaches of the Fair Trading and Commerce Acts. It claims Clear's customers are being "hijacked" by deceptive and misleading conduct. People who used its system to make toll colls had been switched over to Telecom without having given permission, it said. Page 1.

Business has said a firm "no thanks" to plans to turn the clock back with $100 million of handouts pledged under the Coalition agreement. The proposals include $50 million for an export gaurantee fund, $10 million for a venture capital fund, $5 million more for Tradenz and $32 million for organic farming. The four major industry associations say the money would be better spent on further tax reductions rather than poorly thought out handouts to companies which are unlikely to be internationally competetive. Page 1.

The listed US company at the centre of an encryption export row involving the top secret Government Communications Security Bureau says its business plans have been badly hit by a delay in getting access to New Zealnd-developed encryption software. New York-based Cyphercom Solutions has warned it might have to file for bankruptcy because of financial problems partly inflenced by the delay. Page 1.

The Phoenix Flock Co No 1 Ltd ostrich float has been abondoned due to lack of investor support. A prospectus was issued last August by promoters Bryan Bassett Smith, Earle Embrey, Mervyn Huxford, and John and Diana Stil. The key person was Embrey, an Austalian ostrich farmer, who was to sell progeny into the $2.7 million venture. Part of the problem was a requirement under the Securities Act to value the birds at fixed prices. This proved to be over-priced as the market declined last year. Page 3.

Serious Fraud Office director Charles Sturt was allegedly abusive of Winston Peters in SFO staff meetings, nearly two years before the MP upped the ante by accusing the SFO of possible corruption. The issue came under a new focus at the winebox inquiry this week as commission lawyers probed whether Surt allowed a personal animosity towrad Peters to cloud the SFO's judgement on the winebox and other related complaints. Page 9.

The stepped-up US attack on the Diary Board's status defies logic, Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith says. And board executive Nigel Mitchell finds "a fair deal of hypocrisy" in it. They point out that the American dairy maket is among the most closed in the world to imports, its dairy farmers remain heavily subsidised and the US Department of Agriculture operates billion dollar export subsidy and credit schemes that distort international trade. Despite this, the board is a leading target for American attack in the lead-up to the next round of agricultural trade liberalisation negotiations. Page 12.

Support for reintroducing the death penalty as a possible sentence for murder has grown significantly, with more than three out of five voters now backing such a move. The latest NBR-Consultus poll asked people whether they thought the death penalty should be reintroduced for "some murders". Sixty-three percent said yes, 33 percent no and four percent were unsure. In January 1992 the figures were respectively 52 percent, 44 percent and four percent. Page 14.

Macraes Mining Co's strong fourth-quarter performance and ever-more-promising outlook have pushed the company's biggest shareholder away from takeover rumours. Union Gold Mining, controlled by Brett Fogarty of Perth, has been involved in Macraes since 1987 and holds 38 percent of the company, which produces gold from eastern Otago and is working toward production at Reefton. Its 1996 output enabled Macraes to more than double pretax profit to $23 million. Page 41.

More fights between the hog and the dog are in the wind. Clear Communications (represented in advertisements by a bouncy blue pig) and Telecom Corporation (invariably associated with an athletic terrier) are poised for further legal action. This is connected to the former's recent statement that it would never be undercut by its arch rival. "As of today you will never have to wonder which phone company to use for national toll calls," said a voice as the pig danced jerkily across our TV screens. Clear guarantees that we will never be undersold by Telecom on any natinally advertised 'talk as long as you like' residential toll offers like $5 weeks or $2.95 weekends." But to this
cynical correspondent, the offer seemed unusual. Page 55.
